before: Animal-vehicle collisions are far more common than many drivers realize. According to the Insurance Information Institute, there are more than one million car accidents involving animals each year in the United States, causing thousands of injuries and over 200 deaths annually. In Georgia and South Carolina — where deer populations are substantial and rural highways are common — understanding how your car insurance applies to these accidents is critical for protecting yourself financially.
after: Animal-vehicle collisions are far more common than many drivers realize. According to State Farm, drivers made more than 1.6 million animal-collision insurance claims nationwide between July 2025 and June 2026, and the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety counted 210 deaths in animal-collision crashes in 2024. In Georgia and South Carolina — where deer populations are substantial and rural highways are common — understanding how your car insurance applies to these accidents is critical for protecting yourself financially.

before:
• Deer strikes — The most frequent animal collision in both Georgia and South Carolina, especially during fall mating season (October through December)
  • Livestock encounters — Cattle, horses, and other farm animals that escape fenced pastures and wander onto roads
  • Stray dog and cat collisions — Common in suburban and urban areas, particularly at dusk and dawn
  • Swerve-to-avoid accidents — Drivers who swerve to miss an animal and strike another vehicle, guardrail, tree, or ditch
  • Wild boar and feral hog crossings — An increasing problem in rural areas of both states

Georgia consistently ranks among the top 15 states for deer-vehicle collisions, while South Carolina's Lowcountry and Upstate regions see high volumes of wildlife crossings year-round. Highways like US-17 along the coast and I-26 through rural South Carolina are particularly prone to animal encounters.

before: Under Georgia law, livestock owners have a duty to keep their animals properly fenced and confined (O.C.G.A. § 4-3-3). If cattle, horses, or other livestock escape due to the owner's negligence and cause a car accident, the animal owner may be held liable for your injuries and vehicle damage.
after: Georgia makes it unlawful for an owner to let livestock run at large on a public road (O.C.G.A. § 4-3-3). Liability is not automatic: you must show negligence, but an animal loose on the road lets a jury infer the owner was negligent unless the owner proves ordinary care in confining it. If cattle, horses, or other livestock escape due to the owner's negligence and cause a car accident, the animal owner may be held liable for your injuries and vehicle damage.

before:
South Carolina's livestock laws require animal owners to keep their animals properly enclosed. Under S.C. Code § 47-7-120, livestock owners can be held liable when their animals escape and cause accidents on public roadways. Counties may also have local fence ordinances that impose additional requirements.

In both states, the minimum required auto insurance does not include comprehensive or collision coverage — only liability. Georgia requires minimum liability of 25/50/25 (O.C.G.A. § 33-7-11), while South Carolina requires 25/50/25 (S.C. Code § 38-77-140). Without optional comprehensive coverage, you have no insurance protection for animal strike damage to your own vehicle.
after:
South Carolina makes it unlawful for an owner wilfully or negligently to let any domestic animal run at large beyond the owner's own land (S.C. Code § 47-7-110). The South Carolina Supreme Court has held that an animal loose on the highway is not enough by itself; you must offer evidence from which a jury could find the owner negligent in letting it stray (Reed v. Clark, 277 S.C. 310 (1982)).

In both states, the minimum required auto insurance does not include comprehensive or collision coverage — only liability coverage, plus uninsured motorist coverage in South Carolina (S.C. Code § 38-77-150). Georgia requires minimum liability of 25/50/25 (O.C.G.A. § 33-7-11), while South Carolina requires 25/50/25 (S.C. Code § 38-77-140). Without optional comprehensive coverage, you have no insurance protection for animal strike damage to your own vehicle.

1. Pull over safely — Move your vehicle to the shoulder if possible. Turn on your hazard lights to alert other drivers
  2. Call 911 — Report the accident, especially if there are injuries, significant vehicle damage, or the animal is blocking the roadway. A police report strengthens your insurance claim
  3. Do not approach the animal — Injured animals can be dangerous and unpredictable. Wait for animal control or wildlife officers
  4. Document the scene — Photograph your vehicle damage, the animal (if safe to do so), road conditions, and the location. Note the time, visibility conditions, and weather
  5. Check for injuries — Seek medical attention for yourself and any passengers, even if injuries seem minor. Head injuries and whiplash may not present symptoms immediately
  6. Contact your insurance company — File a comprehensive claim (for direct animal strikes) or collision claim (for swerve accidents) promptly
  7. If livestock was involved — Try to identify the animal's owner. Check for brands, ear tags, or nearby farms. This information is critical if you need to pursue a liability claim against the owner

after: In both Georgia and South Carolina, a driver who swerves may be found partially or fully at fault if their reaction was unreasonable under the circumstances. Both states recognize the sudden-emergency doctrine: a driver who reacts reasonably to an animal that appears without warning is not held to perfect judgment, but the doctrine does not protect a driver whose own speed or inattention created the emergency (Stephens v.   • Prior escapes — If the animal had escaped before, the owner had notice of the fencing deficiency

before: Hitting an animal directly is covered by comprehensive insurance, while swerving into another object falls under collision coverage. Livestock owners can be liable under O.C.G.A. § 4-3-3 (Georgia) and S.C. Code § 47-7-120 (South Carolina). Georgia allows 2 years for injury claims (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33) and South Carolina allows 3 years (S.C. Code § 15-3-530). Minimum liability-only insurance does not cover animal strike damage to your vehicle.

Georgia allows 2 years for injury claims (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33) and South Carolina allows 3 years (S.C. Code § 15-3-530). Minimum liability-only insurance does not cover animal strike damage to your vehicle.
